bridges.description: Support the existence of the classical-theist God identified as necessary unlimited being with intellect, will, and perfect goodness.
Infer from contingent reality and the principle of sufficient reason to a necessary ground of existence.
Infer from a finite temporal universe to an immaterial, timeless, powerful, and personal cause.
Treat life-permitting order and fine-tuned constants as evidence of purposive design.
Infer from objective moral facts, equal dignity, and intrinsic prohibitions to perfect goodness as their ground.
Withhold the classical-theist conclusion unless its premises and its advantage over naturalistic and supernaturalistic alternatives are established.
Challenge the warrant for contingency, temporal-beginning, fine-tuning, and moral premises without adopting a burden to prove that no conceivable god exists.
Require probability-sensitive comparison of theism with the full range of relevant alternatives rather than a move from possibility or generic supernaturalism.
Treat nonresistant nonbelief and gratuitous suffering as probabilistic evidence favoring naturalism or different God concepts over classical theism.
Keep polytheism, deism, quasi-deism, pantheism, pandeism, and other monotheisms live as distinct rival explanations.

sections.title: Burdens and inference method
sections.rationale: The debate repeatedly turns on what each side must establish, whether deductive premises must be uncontroversial, and when probabilistic comparison is required.

sections.title: Contingency and necessary being
sections.rationale: Horn's first route supplies his proposed ultimate ground, while Lataster disputes both the world's contingency and the move from a necessary reality to the specified God.

sections.title: Finite origin and theories of time
sections.rationale: The temporal beginning argument and the dispute over eternalist theories form a distinct causal route with sustained replies and clarification.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and design
sections.rationale: Life-permitting constants provide Horn's design route and invite Lataster's challenges about probability, alternative life, and explanatory comparison.

sections.title: Morality, suffering, and hiddenness
sections.rationale: Objective morality is Horn's route to perfect goodness, while suffering and nonresistant nonbelief are Lataster's main positive probabilistic evidence.

sections.title: Rival God concepts and classical theism
sections.rationale: A central dispute is whether the arguments reach one unlimited, personal, perfectly good God or leave numerous supernatural alternatives live.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The affirmative answers yes to God's existence and concerns an immaterial, pure, unlimited being that grounds all existence rather than a physical object within the universe.
moves.warrant: Science does not settle every question of existence, including immaterial realities, while philosophy addresses fundamental reality.
moves.inference: The motion may be addressed by philosophical arguments whose target is the classical-theist ground Horn defines.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage begins with Horn's statement of the motion and burden and ends where he introduces his four proposed effects, preserving the definition that controls his later routes.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the most basic reality that grounds all of existence
Pure Unlimited being that exists without deficiency
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator has handed the opening to Horn, and uninterrupted first-person continuity identifies him throughout.
moves.importanceRationale: It fixes the affirmative target and the inference method for every later argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It states Horn's affirmative answer and specifies the God whose existence he undertakes to support.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Because the contingent universe exists, its explanation terminates in a necessary reality that exists by its nature and cannot fail to exist.
moves.warrant: Horn invokes the principle of sufficient reason, argues that the universe and its parts could have failed to exist, and says an infinite series of contingent things would leave the same explanatory question.
moves.inference: A necessary ground of all contingent existence is identified with pure existence or unlimited being.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Horn's complete first route from sufficient reason through the universe's alleged contingency and rejection of an infinite contingent regress to the attributes he attaches to the necessary ground.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there must be a reality that is necessary
a reality that exists by its very nature
moves.attributionRationale: This is Horn's uninterrupted opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: This is a central independent route and later supplies Horn's answer to rival God concepts.

burdenContact.rationale: It provides the full inference from contingent existence to a necessary ground.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe began to exist and therefore has a cause beyond space, time, matter, and energy.
moves.warrant: Horn appeals to causal intuition, reports scientific evidence leaning toward an absolute beginning, and argues that an actually infinite past could not be traversed successively.
moves.inference: The cause is said to be immaterial, eternal, powerful, and personal because it creates the entire physical order and chooses a finite universe.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete finite-beginning route, including causal premise, scientific and philosophical support, and the attributes inferred for the cause; trimming any of those elements would omit a disputed load-bearing step.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: out of nothing nothing comes
the past is not in and instead there's a beginning of time
moves.attributionRationale: Horn remains the sole speaker in his opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a separate central causal route and becomes the focus of the time-theory exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It states and supports the beginning-to-cause inference and its claimed divine attributes.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Life-permitting constants exhibit predictable order that is better explained by design than by chance or necessity.
moves.warrant: Horn reports extreme sensitivity in constants, argues that chance would be extraordinarily improbable, and says their necessity has not been demonstrated.
moves.inference: If neither chance nor necessity explains the values, an agent setting the universe's early conditions is offered as the remaining explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span covers Horn's complete third route from life-permitting constants through his chance and necessity comparisons to the proposed designing agent.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the universe contains predictable order
an unknown agent set the early conditions
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is continuously speaking in his opening.
moves.importanceRationale: Fine-tuning is one of Horn's four independent affirmative routes.

burdenContact.rationale: It is Horn's direct bridge from observed order to agency.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Objective moral facts exist, including equal human dignity and acts that remain wrong regardless of consequences, and perfect goodness explains them.
moves.warrant: Horn appeals to moral reasoning and perception, argues that unequal cognitive capacities cannot ground equal rights, and contrasts intrinsic prohibitions with purely outcome-based rules.
moves.inference: A perfectly good source that bestows equal intrinsic value and grounds human natures explains these moral facts.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This long span is required to preserve the complete moral route: the defense of moral realism, the equal-dignity application, the intrinsic-evil application, and the concluding appeal to God as perfect goodness. These are linked stages rather than free-standing repetitions.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are certain moral facts
morality comes from God who is by nature perfect goodness itself
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is the uninterrupted opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the route Horn uses to reach perfect goodness rather than merely a generic cause.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies Horn's complete inference from moral facts to their perfectly good ground.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: As an agnostic non-theist, Lataster rejects a burden to prove that no God exists while accepting the task of challenging the specified God of classical theism.
moves.warrant: He distinguishes non-theism from a positive denial and lists the target's classical attributes, including knowledge, power, goodness, creation, necessity, and desired human relationship.
moves.inference: The affirmative retains responsibility for establishing that specified concept, while Lataster may defeat the case by challenging its premises or comparative support.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Lataster's complete burden clarification and his identification of the exact classical-theist target before he begins replying to individual routes.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I am agnostic you can call me agnostic if you like
the God we're talking about is not just any generic God
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator has handed the negative opening to Lataster, whose first-person continuity is clear.
moves.importanceRationale: It determines the negative's adopted burden and prevents treating agnosticism as a positive universal denial.

burdenContact.rationale: It defines the negative route as withholding the specified conclusion while challenging its support.

responseComponents.description: Rejects Horn's proposed negative burden and accepts the same classical-theist target.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: The contingency and beginning arguments do not establish their crucial premises because neither the world's contingency nor its beginning is known.
moves.warrant: Lataster says necessity has not been excluded, the Big Bang describes expansion rather than creation from nothing, and the philosophical beginning argument depends on a contested theory of time.
moves.inference: Without adequate warrant for contingency or a finite beginning, the deductive routes cannot establish their conclusions.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact sequence replies to the contingency route and then the finite-beginning route, ending with the distinct time-theory objection that is later clarified in cross-examination.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we don't actually know that the world is contingent
the Big Bang doesn't actually prove that the Universe came into existence
moves.attributionRationale: Speaker continuity is clear, but automatic captions corrupt scientific names and the phrase concerning substance dualism and nothingness.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify the scientific names and technical wording if any exact public quotation is drawn from this passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests premises in two of the affirmative's central routes.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the uncertain premises Lataster says the affirmative must support.

responseComponents.description: Disputes knowledge that the world is contingent or that God is necessary.
Distinguishes cosmic expansion from creation from nothing and raises a live time-theory alternative.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Fine-tuning does not yield intelligent design merely because chance and necessity are treated as unsupported options.
moves.warrant: Lataster argues that the ordering of alternatives is arbitrary, that necessity has not been excluded, and that different constants might permit other forms of life.
moves.inference: Design cannot win by default without a comparative probability analysis and justified assumptions about the range of possible life.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage is Lataster's full opening reply to fine-tuning, from the alleged default inference through necessity and alternative-life objections.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you could put intelligent design right at the start
there's no evidence whatsoever that changing the constants couldn't yield some other form of Life
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster remains the sole opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Horn's only design-specific route.

burdenContact.rationale: It demands a non-arbitrary comparison among chance, necessity, and design.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the elimination of chance and necessity and the assumption that only familiar life is relevant.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Neither objective morality nor its dependence on God has been established.
moves.warrant: Lataster says moral facts might be absent or might instead be a feature of the universe, and he argues that Horn appeals to subjective reactions to establish objectivity.
moves.inference: The moral observations do not yet select God as their required explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Lataster's focused opening reply to both premises of Horn's moral route, ending before he changes to the broader deductive-method dispute.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we don't know that objective morality exists
nor do we know that if objective morality exists it has anything to do with God
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster is continuously speaking.
moves.importanceRationale: It attacks the existence and grounding premises of Horn's route to perfect goodness.

burdenContact.rationale: It states why Lataster withholds the two load-bearing moral premises.

responseComponents.description: Challenges both moral realism and the claimed inference from moral facts to God.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Horn's deductive case fails unless its premises are accepted, and any resulting generic supernaturalism must still be compared probabilistically with contrary evidence and alternative explanations.
moves.warrant: Lataster distinguishes deductive validity from warrant for premises and says a probabilistic case requires likelihoods, evidence against, and rival supernatural hypotheses.
moves.inference: Even successful generic arguments would not alone establish classical theism without the comparative step.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves Lataster's full method argument: premise acceptance, the deductive/probabilistic distinction, the demand for contrary evidence, and the gap between supernaturalism and theism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if we don't accept the premises the argument doesn't work
it's not a deductive case for theism
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster is the uninterrupted speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the methodological bridge supporting his later alternative-concept case.

burdenContact.rationale: It specifies the additional comparative work Lataster says is required.

responseComponents.description: Disputes that presenting deductive routes alone satisfies the affirmative burden.
Says a generic supernatural conclusion would still require comparison with alternatives.
Includes the causal route among arguments that require warranted premises and comparative assessment.
Requires explicit probabilities and alternative explanations.
Requires the moral premises and inference to be warranted rather than merely possible.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Nonresistant nonbelief and gratuitous suffering are probabilistic evidence favoring naturalism or a different God concept over classical theism.
moves.warrant: Lataster argues that a revelatory, all-good, all-knowing, all-powerful God makes such observations less expected, while naturalism predicts them more readily.
moves.inference: These observations shift comparative probability without logically disproving every God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains both positive negative-side evidential routes and Lataster's explicit qualification that hiddenness does not prove God's nonexistence but moves the scale probabilistically.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it doesn't prove that God doesn't exist
gratuitous suffering it doesn't make sense
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster is the sole opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: These are Lataster's principal positive observations against the specified classical-theist concept.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly presents the two observations as probabilistic burden contact.

responseComponents.description: Tests the specified classical-theist attributes against expected revelation.
Uses suffering as evidence against the all-good attribute Horn seeks to infer.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Even granting supernaturalism and then monotheism for argument's sake leaves polytheism, deism, quasi-deism, alternative monotheisms, pantheism, and pandeism as live rivals to classical theism.
moves.warrant: Lataster argues that simplicity has not been quantified, some alternatives require fewer added assumptions, and hiddenness or suffering may be more expected under nonrevelatory or morally different gods.
moves.inference: Without deductively excluding or probabilistically comparing these rivals, generic supernatural evidence does not establish classical theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This extended span is necessary because Lataster deliberately constructs a taxonomy of distinct rivals—polytheistic, alternative-monotheistic, deistic, quasi-deistic, pantheistic, and mixed—and gives separate prior or likelihood reasons for each. Splitting it would obscure his catch-all comparison and conditional grants.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are infinitely many supernaturalistic Alternatives
theism can't even be said to be the best monotheism
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster's speaker continuity is clear, but automatic captions corrupt several technical labels, especially deism, quasi-deism, pantheism, and pandeism.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify technical God-concept labels before using exact public wording from this span.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Lataster's central distinctive argument against moving from generic supernaturalism to classical theism.

burdenContact.rationale: It enumerates and motivates the rival concepts the affirmative must distinguish.

responseComponents.description: Argues that a necessary ground does not by itself select classical theism from rival supernatural concepts.
Treats the causal conclusion as compatible with alternatives.
Allows that design evidence could be explained by many agents or God concepts.
Offers morally indifferent or differently good concepts as comparative rivals.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Deductive arguments need reasonable support for their premises, not unanimous acceptance, and Lataster has not shown that a reasonable person must reject Horn's premises.
moves.warrant: Horn notes that any premise can be denied and distinguishes mere disagreement from an argument showing a premise false or the inference invalid.
moves.inference: The affirmative routes remain live unless their premises or logical steps receive substantive answers.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage contains Horn's complete reply to Lataster's methodological burden, ending exactly as he turns to the contingency argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: anyone can deny a premise in an argument
he needs to show that a reasonable person can reject my premises
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator has introduced Horn's first rebuttal, and Horn speaks continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It frames how Horn asks the audience to evaluate all subsequent replies.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the standard of support Horn claims is sufficient to discharge his affirmative burden.

responseComponents.description: Rejects unanimous or uncontroversial acceptance as the standard and asks for substantive premise or inference objections.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe's possible nonexistence and composition from contingent objects support its contingency, while necessity is part of the proposed being's definition rather than proof of its existence.
moves.warrant: Horn repeats his modal and composition reasons and distinguishes asking whether a necessary being exists from defining such a being into existence.
moves.inference: Lataster's objections do not yet remove the contingency route's explanatory terminus.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This focused span answers Lataster's two contingency objections and preserves Horn's definition-versus-existence distinction before he moves to the beginning argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm not defining God into existence
a necessary being that grounds all of reality
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is the sole rebuttal speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It defends the modal premise and a key distinction needed by Horn's central route.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly repairs the challenged contingency and necessity steps.

responseComponents.description: Restates reasons for the universe's contingency and distinguishes defining the candidate ground from establishing that it exists.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Scientific and philosophical support for a beginning remains, and citing a rival theory of time or dissenting physicists does not itself refute that support.
moves.warrant: Horn appeals again to beginning-oriented cosmological claims, says the philosophical argument was untouched, and notes that the B theory is not universally accepted.
moves.inference: The finite-beginning premise remains sufficiently supported for his causal inference.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage is Horn's complete first-rebuttal defense of the beginning argument, including scientific and time-theory responses, ending before fine-tuning begins.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the philosophical arguments have not been touched
we haven't seen any arguments that show the first cause argument doesn't exist
moves.attributionRationale: Horn's ownership is clear, but captions corrupt physicist names and contain a likely recognition error in the quoted conclusion about the argument.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify technical names and avoid the captioned phrase about an argument 'doesn't exist' as a featured quotation.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves Horn's main answer to the temporal-beginning critique.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends both scientific and philosophical support for a finite past.

responseComponents.description: Answers the cosmology and contested-time-theory objections to a finite beginning.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Subjective access does not make moral facts subjective, and ordinary moral perception supplies defeasible justification for objective moral truth.
moves.warrant: Horn analogizes moral knowledge to mathematical and external-world knowledge and argues that Lataster's language of gratuitous suffering itself invokes a way things ought to be.
moves.inference: The moral route remains available, and evil can presuppose rather than eliminate objective moral order.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage includes Horn's epistemology-versus-ontology distinction and his reply that the suffering objection uses normative judgment.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we only know math through our subjective thoughts
there's a way things are supposed to be
moves.attributionRationale: Horn speaks continuously in rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers both Lataster's moral epistemology objection and the normative basis of his suffering argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the existence and knowability of the moral facts on which Horn relies.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes subjective cognition from the objectivity of what is known.
Argues that calling suffering gratuitous invokes objective normative standards.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: An ultimate necessary explanation cannot be limited or divided among competing deities, and uniform natural order points to one source rather than many.
moves.warrant: Horn argues that limits would themselves require explanation, that multiple ultimate beings would compromise ultimacy, and that pantheism would identify the cause with what is caused.
moves.inference: The contingency and order routes are said to narrow generic supernaturalism to one unlimited source and exclude polytheism and pantheism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Horn's unified reply to the rival-concept challenge, preserving his limitation, unity, order, pantheism, and deism claims as the linked narrowing argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the cause of reality cannot be limited in any way
one universal source
moves.attributionRationale: Horn remains the only rebuttal speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Horn's principal attempt to bridge from generic supernaturalism to classical monotheism.

burdenContact.rationale: It uses the necessary-ground route to argue for uniqueness and absence of limitation.

responseComponents.description: Offers uniqueness, uniform order, and cause-effect distinctions against polytheism, pantheism, and deism.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Deism, quasi-deism, pantheism, and other catch-all alternatives remain live because Horn has not shown that revelation or creation from nothing is required.
moves.warrant: Lataster says a nonrevelatory God adds fewer claims, an eternal universe avoids pantheism causing itself, and many variants fit the evidence without substance dualism or creation from nothing.
moves.inference: Horn still needs a comparative probability analysis rather than a brief dismissal of each class of rivals.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span covers Lataster's complete first-rebuttal defense of deism, quasi-deism, and pantheistic families, including why the conditional eternal-universe response matters.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: deism is a serious rival to theism
there's not just one pantheism
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster's speaker continuity is clear, but caption recognition repeatedly corrupts technical God-concept terms.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify deism, quasi-deism, pantheism, and creation-from-nothing terminology before exact publication.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Horn's main narrowing response and retains multiple independently relevant alternatives.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why the named rival families have not been excluded.

responseComponents.description: Rejects Horn's deism and pantheism dismissals and reasserts the need to compare whole families of alternatives.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: His own willing nonbelief is less expected if an all-good, all-powerful, all-knowing God desires his salvation and relationship.
moves.warrant: Lataster says such a God would want to convince him, would know what would do so, and would have the power to provide it, yet has not.
moves.inference: Either classical theism is false or a different kind of God better fits the observed nonbelief.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage presents Lataster's complete nonresistant-nonbelief example and explicitly connects the observation to naturalism and alternative God concepts.

moves.importanceRationale: It makes the hiddenness argument concrete and connects each classical attribute to the expected revelation.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the central case offered as probabilistic evidence from hiddenness.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Nonbelief is compatible with God if God has reasons to permit it, including free choice, believers sharing the good of testimony, and salvation without explicit belief.
moves.warrant: Horn proposes that overwhelming manifestation could affect free choice and notes his tradition's view that nonbelief through no fault of one's own does not entail damnation.
moves.inference: Lataster has not shown that nonresistant nonbelief is sufficiently unexpected on theism to defeat it.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Horn's complete second-rebuttal answer to hiddenness, including all three reasons the frozen source requires preserving.

moves.importanceRationale: It is Horn's only developed response to Lataster's central positive hiddenness evidence.

responseComponents.description: Offers freedom, shared testimony, and nonautomatic damnation as reasons God might permit nonbelief.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The contingency and moral routes jointly identify an unlimited, personal, perfectly good foundation rather than an indifferent deistic or plural divine reality.
moves.warrant: Horn says a limited ultimate explanation would be contingent and that moral facts concern how things ought to be, requiring purposive perfect goodness rather than descriptive natural law alone.
moves.inference: The convergence of the routes is offered as the bridge from generic supernaturalism to classical theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Horn's second-round synthesis of necessary unlimited being, personal design, and perfect goodness, followed by his is-versus-ought reason for resisting a natural moral ground.

burdenContact.rationale: It combines the central routes to reach the motion's specified conclusion.

moves.inference: Failure to establish the comparative superiority of theism is enough to resist the affirmative conclusion.

moves.claim: A deductive argument can be rationally used when its premises are more likely true than false and the inference is valid, without certainty or universal agreement.
moves.warrant: Horn distinguishes deductive form from certainty about premises and says neither fallacies nor adequate contrary evidence have been shown in his routes.
moves.inference: The absence of certainty does not force him to replace his arguments with a numerical probabilistic case.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This cross-examination answer directly addresses Lataster's demand for probabilistic reasoning and states Horn's actual standard for deductive premises.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the premises are more likely to be true than false
a deductive argument is a fine way to argue
moves.attributionRationale: Horn's extended answer is identifiable, though the questioner and respondent briefly overlap in the rapid exchange.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify exact handoffs if a longer quotation is selected from this mixed cross-examination.
moves.importanceRationale: It resolves a central dispute over whether deductive form requires certainty.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the evidential standard by which Horn says his affirmative case succeeds.

responseComponents.description: Rejects certainty as necessary for rational acceptance of deductive premises.
Maintains that Horn may defend his own route without adopting Lataster's numerical framework.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: An infinite temporal collection differs from God's qualitative lack of limitation, so rejecting an infinite past is not inconsistent with calling God infinite or eternal.
moves.warrant: Horn says successive physical collections generate the relevant infinity problem, whereas God's infinity means that knowledge, power, and existence lack limits and God's eternity is timeless rather than an endless sequence.
moves.inference: The proposed cause can be timeless and unlimited even if the temporal universe cannot have an actually infinite past.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This cross-examination span preserves the precise mathematical-or-collection versus qualitative-infinity distinction and Horn's account of timeless eternity.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are different kinds of infinity
God is not limited
moves.attributionRationale: Horn's response is extended and coherent, though brief questions frame both ends of the mixed exchange.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify the transition into and out of Horn's answer if a longer excerpt is used.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers a direct internal-consistency challenge to the finite-past route.

burdenContact.rationale: It preserves the distinction needed to infer a timeless cause from a finite temporal collection.

responseComponents.description: Explains why divine eternity is not the same structure as an infinite temporal past.
Reasserts Horn's conceptual distinction even while eternalist theories remain disputed.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Taken together, contingency, finite cause, fine-tuning, and morality converge on one unlimited, necessary, perfectly good source rather than merely unspecified supernaturalism.
moves.warrant: Horn argues that plurality reintroduces contingency, uniform order favors one source, and objective moral facts require a perfectly good personal ground.
moves.inference: The combined routes are offered as sufficient support for the classical-theist conclusion.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing span contains Horn's final synthesis across all four routes and his explicit response to the claim that the arguments establish only generic supernaturalism; it excludes later exhortation and does not import excluded Q&A answers as independent support.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: only one unlimited reality provides necessary foundations
objective moral facts that could only come from a perfectly good person
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator clearly introduces Horn's closing, and he speaks continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the affirmative's final motion-level convergence argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It states why Horn thinks his separate bridges jointly establish the motion.

responseComponents.description: Argues that uniqueness, order, and goodness narrow the conclusion beyond generic supernaturalism.
Claims the accumulated evidence is sufficient despite Lataster's continued agnosticism.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: His grants of supernaturalism and monotheism were conditional debate concessions, not beliefs, and the affirmative still has not shown classical theism superior to alternative supernatural concepts.
moves.warrant: Lataster reiterates that suffering and hiddenness are probabilistic rather than logical disproofs, that deistic and quasi-deistic rivals differ principally over revelation, and that even an ontological route would conditionally favor an unrestricted pantheistic concept in his view.
moves.inference: Because the arguments can fit other supernatural hypotheses, a comparative analysis remains necessary before affirming classical theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The complete closing is required to preserve Lataster's explicit withdrawal of the conditional grant, his non-disproof qualification, his distinctions among deism, quasi-deism, and pantheism, and the stable conditional ontological-to-pantheistic inference despite a nearby self-correction in the captions.

if they do work they lead to pantheism
